explanation: Cutting breaks open cells, letting an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase react with oxygen in the air. Lemon juice slows the browning, because its acid holds the enzyme back.

claims.text: Cut apples turn brown when the enzyme polyphenol oxidase reacts with oxygen.
The browning of a freshly cut apple is not caused by bacteria, sunlight or melting sugar.
Cutting an apple ruptures cells, bringing the enzyme into contact with compounds and oxygen.
Lemon juice slows browning, mainly because its acidity inhibits the enzyme.

evidence.restatement: Cut apples brown when polyphenol oxidase uses oxygen to oxidize the fruit's phenolic compounds into brown pigments.

claimResults.note: Strictly, the enzyme catalyses the reaction of phenols with oxygen rather than reacting with oxygen itself; the claim simplifies it.

evidence.restatement: The browning is not caused by bacteria, sunlight or melting sugar.
Cutting ruptures cells and brings the enzyme, its phenolic substrates and oxygen together.
Lemon juice's low pH (about 2) slows polyphenol oxidase, which works best near neutral pH; its vitamin C also helps by reducing the coloured products.

claimResults.note: Citric acid far outweighs vitamin C in lemon juice, so acidity as the main reason is defensible.

issues.note: Explanation: 'letting an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase react with oxygen' simplifies the chemistry; 'letting an enzyme, polyphenol oxidase, use oxygen in the air to oxidize the fruit's phenols' is exact if the editor wants it.

evidence.restatement: Polyphenol oxidase acts on phenolic compounds with oxygen to brown cut apple.
Bacteria, sunlight and melting sugar are not the cause.
Cutting ruptures cells and lets the enzyme meet its substrates and oxygen.
Lemon juice slows browning, partly because its acidity inhibits the enzyme.

claimResults.note: Vitamin C in the juice also helps by reducing the brown products, so 'mainly because its acidity' is a simplification; the explanation's own wording (its acid holds the enzyme back) is acceptable.
